slides.title: The Development of the English Common Law
Where this stands against the ius commune
slides.text: The lecture opens by naming the contrast it is built on. On the continent: reception of Roman law, the ius commune as a general law created by LEARNED JURISTS, a mixture of domestic customary law, statutes and ius commune, and repeated attempts to bring those sources into a hierarchy. In England: the development of a common law with SOME SIMILARITIES but a VERY DIFFERENT OUTCOME. Keep the question open as you go through the slides — what exactly made the difference, given that England had Roman law available too?

cards.q: What is the question the lecture on the common law is built around?
cards.a: Why England produced a very different outcome from the continent, when the starting materials were similar — customary law, statutes and available Roman law. On the continent learned jurists built the ius commune; in England the royal courts built a case law.

slides.title: The Laws of Æthelberht (7th century)
slides.text: The earliest written legal document so far known for England: legal provisions written in OLD ENGLISH — not Latin — setting compensation and punishment for personal injury, with the aim of REPLACING BLOOD FEUDS. Written laws in Old English then increase immensely until the 9th century. Two things to notice for later: the vernacular, and the fact that the earliest English law is about buying off vengeance.

cards.q: What are the Laws of Æthelberht, and what two features matter?
cards.a: The earliest known written legal document of England, 7th century: compensation and punishment for personal injury, aimed at replacing blood feuds. Notable because it is written in Old English — the vernacular, not Latin — and because the earliest English law is about buying off vengeance.

slides.title: The Norman invasion, 1066
slides.text: The Normans conquer England under William the Conqueror and establish a new kingdom: CENTRALIZED government, with most positions held by Normans. And the first act of continuity — a COMPILATION of the existing laws and customs. That combination, a foreign conquering dynasty that immediately writes down what was already there, is what the 17th century will later argue about.

cards.q: What did the Norman conquest of 1066 bring, and what did it preserve?
cards.a: A new kingdom with centralized government and most offices in Norman hands — and, as a first act of continuity, a compilation of the laws and customs already in existence.

slides.title: England did have Roman law
slides.text: The point that kills the easy explanation. Reception of Roman law in England STARTS — with Vacarius, who had studied at Bologna and taught at Oxford in the 12th century. The Corpus Iuris Civilis becomes available in England in the 12th century, the study of Roman law expands from Oxford to other centres, and many Englishmen study on the continent. So England is not a place Roman law failed to reach. Whatever explains the different outcome, it is not ignorance of Roman law.

terms.def: Bologna-trained jurist who taught Roman law at Oxford in the 12th century — the beginning of the reception of Roman law in England.

cards.q: Was Roman law unknown in England?
cards.a: No. Its reception began with Vacarius, Bologna-trained, teaching at Oxford in the 12th century; the Corpus Iuris Civilis was available in England from the 12th century, its study spread from Oxford, and many Englishmen studied on the continent. The different outcome cannot be explained by ignorance of Roman law.

slides.title: Royal justice as an alternative, not a hierarchy
slides.text: The web of royal justice grows steadily between the 11th and 13th centuries, driven by the centralized government of the crown and the idea that the crown is RESPONSIBLE FOR GRANTING PEACE — which in practice limits the power of the lords. It expands first where litigants are physically next to the court, then temporally, later geographically. And the decisive structural fact: royal justice did NOT stand in a hierarchical order above the ecclesiastical, local and feudal courts. It stood BESIDE them as an ALTERNATIVE, and every free man could choose to bring his case to it. Royal justice grew by being chosen, not by being imposed.

cards.q: What was the relationship between royal justice and the ecclesiastical, local and feudal courts in England?
cards.a: Not hierarchical. Royal justice stood beside them as an ALTERNATIVE, and every free man could choose to take his case there. It therefore grew by being chosen rather than by being imposed from above.

cards.q: What justified the expansion of royal justice, and whose power did it cut into?
cards.a: The idea that the crown is responsible for granting peace, backed by its centralized government. In practice it limited the power of the lords — which is why the barons later objected to it.

slides.title: Writs and the birth of pleading
slides.text: A WRIT is an order giving instructions how to remedy a situation, and its history is the history of the procedure. At FIRST it was simply issued as an order by royal justice, with no particular procedure attached. In the 12TH CENTURY writs began to allow the wrongdoer to CHOOSE — comply, or defend himself — and out of that choice the procedure of PLEADING arises. By the 13TH CENTURY pleading is a formalized exchange between the parties before the court, followed by a trial in which the parties had to prove the facts on which their claims rested. So the adversarial shape of English procedure grows out of a defendant being given the option to say no.

terms.def: A royal order instructing how a situation is to be remedied — the formal instrument for opening litigation in the royal courts.
The formalized exchange between the parties before the court, arising once writs let a defendant choose to defend rather than comply; followed by the trial of the facts.

cards.q: Trace the writ from a bare order to the procedure of pleading.
cards.a: At first a writ was simply an order of royal justice with no procedure attached. In the 12th century it began letting the wrongdoer choose between complying and defending himself, out of which pleading arose. By the 13th century pleading was a formalized exchange between the parties before the court, followed by a trial of the facts underlying the claims.

slides.title: The writ system consolidates
slides.text: The writ is the FORMAL INSTRUMENT for opening litigation — and at first it depended on the KING'S WILLINGNESS TO INTERVENE, which is to say litigation began as a favour. Standardization runs through the 12th century: orientation on past cases and patterns, and publication of a LIST OF FIXED FORMULAS, so intervention becomes a ROUTINE. The result is the consolidation of royal justice, eventually offering remedies for almost all wrongs. Note the mechanism — a right exists in England if there is a writ for it, so the list of formulas is in effect the catalogue of rights.

cards.q: How did the writ change from a favour into a system?
cards.a: It began as an instrument depending on the king's willingness to intervene. Through the 12th century it was standardized by orientation on past cases and by publishing a list of fixed formulas, so intervention became routine — and royal justice consolidated until it offered a remedy for almost every wrong.

cards.q: In what sense was the list of writs a catalogue of rights?
cards.a: Because a claim could be brought only if a writ fitted it. Where there was no writ there was no remedy, so the fixed formulas effectively defined which rights could be asserted at all.

slides.title: Case law emerges
slides.text: Writs contain rights, and those rights are CREATED THROUGH DECISIONS. From the 13th century there are reports of proceedings in the common law courts — the YEARBOOKS and the PLEA ROLLS — often written by STUDENTS OF LAW, documenting the pleadings and the decisions, and circulating as manuscripts that gave orientation for deciding similar cases. That is case law being born: not by a doctrine of precedent decreed from above, but by practitioners circulating reports of what the courts actually did.

terms.def: Reports of proceedings in the English common law courts from the 13th century, often taken down by law students, circulating in manuscript and guiding the decision of similar cases.

cards.q: How did English case law come into being?
cards.a: Through reports of proceedings — the Yearbooks and Plea Rolls from the 13th century, often written by law students and circulating as manuscripts that guided decisions in similar cases. Precedent grew from practitioners recording what the courts did, not from a doctrine imposed from above.

slides.title: Equity beside the writs
slides.text: An extraordinary remedy system grows up ALONGSIDE the strict writ system: the petitioner addresses the CHANCERY directly. It is at first a flexible system with fluid rules, in its early period often influenced by ROMAN AND CANON law, and later interacting with the common law. But from the 15TH CENTURY it takes on a STATIC character through repetition — patterns of permanent solutions, a list of equity remedies. Equity begins as the answer to the rigidity of the writ system and then hardens in the same way.

terms.def: The extraordinary remedy system addressed to the Chancery beside the strict writ system — at first flexible and influenced by Roman and canon law, from the 15th century itself hardening into a list of remedies.

cards.q: What was equity, and what happened to its flexibility?
cards.a: An extraordinary remedy system beside the strict writ system, addressed directly to the Chancery — at first flexible, with fluid rules, early on influenced by Roman and canon law. From the 15th century repetition made it static: patterns of permanent solutions and a list of equity remedies.

cards.q: Where did Roman law actually operate in England?
cards.a: Above all in the equity courts, whose early flexible practice was often influenced by Roman and canon law — not in the common law courts.

slides.title: Why the common law detached from Roman law
slides.text: Here is the answer to the opening question, and it is about APPOINTMENTS, not ideas. In the 12th and 13th centuries most judges were still trained at the universities or cathedral schools, which means in Roman and canon law. In the 14TH CENTURY the kings' appointment policy CHANGES, because the writ system demands good PRACTICAL knowledge — so judges are increasingly selected from the ADVOCATES WORKING AT THE KING'S COURT. Once the bench is recruited from practitioners rather than from graduates, the learned law loses its route into the judgments. The detachment from Roman law is a by-product of who gets the job.

cards.q: Why did English law detach from Roman law, and when?
cards.a: In the 14th century, through the kings' appointment policy. The writ system demanded practical knowledge, so judges were increasingly chosen from the advocates working at the king's court rather than from university-trained graduates — and the learned law lost its route onto the bench.

slides.title: Royal legislation stayed small
slides.text: Legislation is first issued by the kings; from the 13th and 14th centuries PARLIAMENT proposes responses to petitions, which becomes the basis for legislation. But the verdict is blunt: ALL IN ALL OF MINOR IMPORTANCE. Legislation often only repeated existing norms, and the number of statutes was relatively small compared with the other sources of law. The contrast with the continent, where the early modern era is full of reformations and ordinances, is exactly the point.

cards.q: How important was legislation as a source of English law, and where did it come from?
cards.a: Of minor importance. It was first issued by the kings, then from the 13th–14th centuries grew out of Parliament's responses to petitions — but statutes often merely repeated existing norms and were few compared with the other sources of law.

slides.title: Multinormativity and legal pluralism
slides.text: Two terms the lecture defines, and they are worth keeping apart. MULTINORMATIVITY: the overlap of different normativities in the regulation of ONE ISSUE. LEGAL PLURALISM: overlapping norms within a given TERRITORY that are equally perceived as BINDING. England shows both. Ecclesiastical and feudal courts sit beside royal justice; the crown intervenes by creating royal courts INTO an existing normative system; people could choose whether to go to an ecclesiastical, feudal or royal court — FORUM SHOPPING; and Roman law remained prevalent in the equity courts.

terms.def: The overlap of different normativities in the regulation of one and the same issue.
Overlapping norms within a given territory that are equally perceived as binding.
The litigant's ability to choose which of several available courts — ecclesiastical, feudal or royal — will hear the case.

cards.q: Distinguish multinormativity from legal pluralism.
cards.a: Multinormativity is the overlap of different normativities in the regulation of ONE ISSUE. Legal pluralism is overlapping norms within a given TERRITORY that are equally perceived as binding. The first is about one question, the second about one place.

cards.q: What is forum shopping in the English context, and what made it possible?
cards.a: A litigant choosing between the ecclesiastical, feudal and royal courts. It was possible because royal justice was created INTO an existing normative system as an alternative rather than above it.

slides.title: The common law under pressure
slides.text: From the 14th century criticism grows: the BARONS and feudal lords oppose the continuous expansion of royal justice, and the EQUITY courts become increasingly influential. Then absolutism rises in the 16th and early 17th centuries and the conflict becomes constitutional: common law courts against the crown, culminating in JAMES I's declaration that whenever equity and common law conflict, EQUITY SHOULD PREVAIL. Equity, an extraordinary remedy addressed to the king's Chancellor, has become the crown's instrument against the ordinary courts.

cards.q: What did James I declare about equity and common law, and why did it matter constitutionally?
cards.a: That whenever the two conflicted, equity should prevail. It mattered because equity was addressed to the king's Chancery — so the declaration made the crown's own jurisdiction superior to the ordinary courts, turning a procedural question into a constitutional one.

slides.title: The re-invention of the common law
slides.text: In the 16th and 17th centuries the legal experts — Edward Coke (1552–1634) above all — set out to DETACH the common law from the crown, and they do it with three claims. First, the common law is NOT primarily created by royal intervention but GROUNDED IN CUSTOMS that PREDATED the Norman invasion. Second, it is the ONLY significant legal system that has ever existed in England, superior to all other jurisdictions. Third, it is not merely the law of the royal courts but BINDS THE MONARCH and LIMITS HIS POWER. Notice that all three are historical claims doing constitutional work.

terms.def: 1552–1634, the jurist of the re-invention of the common law: custom older than the Conquest, superior to every other jurisdiction, and binding on the monarch himself.

cards.q: What three claims did Coke and the 16th–17th century lawyers make about the common law?
cards.a: That it is grounded in customs predating the Norman invasion rather than created by royal intervention; that it is the only significant legal system England ever had, superior to all other jurisdictions; and that it binds the monarch and limits his power.

cards.q: Why did lawyers fighting absolutism argue about the Norman Conquest?
cards.a: Because if the common law came from the king, the king could change it. Rooting it in customs older than the Conquest made it independent of royal will — a historical claim doing constitutional work.

slides.title: Re-writing history
slides.text: The re-invention required the past to change shape, and the lecture lists how. The historiography of the Norman invasion changes: the Normans become RESPECTFUL TOWARDS PRE-EXISTING CUSTOMS rather than real conquerors. A narrative is created in which the kings did not actively intervene but PRESERVED old customs. The word 'common' is REDEFINED: common not because it was the KING'S law, but because it was rooted in CUSTOMS. And the whole is re-imagined as free from Roman and canon influence — which, as slide 6 and slide 11 showed, it was not.

cards.q: How was the meaning of 'common' in common law redefined, and by whom?
cards.a: By the 16th–17th century lawyers: common not because it was the KING'S law, applying throughout his realm, but because it was rooted in the CUSTOMS common to the people. The redefinition detaches the law from the crown.

cards.q: Name the historical claims of the re-invention that the earlier slides contradict.
cards.a: That the Normans respected existing customs rather than conquering; that the kings preserved rather than intervened — though royal justice plainly expanded by royal intervention; and that the common law was free of Roman and canon influence — though Roman law reached England with Vacarius in the 12th century and shaped the early equity courts.

slides.title: The common law and constitutional history
slides.text: The summary, and the likeliest essay question of this unit. In the MIDDLE AGES the common law emerges BECAUSE OF the power of the crown and further ENFORCES it, and it is criticised by barons and feudal lords as an offence against their power. In the AGE OF ABSOLUTISM it is detached from the crown and re-invented as a means to LIMIT the king's power by rooting it in tradition and custom, while EQUITY becomes the instrument through which the king seeks to secure power — challenged by the legal experts and judges claiming the supremacy of the common law. The same body of law, the same institutions, and the roles exactly reversed in three centuries.

cards.q: How does the constitutional role of the common law reverse between the Middle Ages and absolutism?
cards.a: In the Middle Ages it emerges from the crown's power and strengthens it, and the barons attack it for that. Under absolutism it is detached from the crown and re-invented as a limit on the king, rooted in custom — while equity, once the flexible remedy, becomes the crown's instrument and is challenged by judges asserting the supremacy of the common law.

cards.q: Who opposed the common law in the Middle Ages, and who defended it under absolutism?
cards.a: In the Middle Ages the barons and feudal lords opposed it, because royal justice cut into their jurisdiction. Under absolutism the legal experts and judges defended it against the crown and its equity jurisdiction.
